claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a native, thin iron-oxide film.
The native oxide on Q235 steel at room temperature is continuous and adherent.
The room-temperature native oxide limits further corrosion of Q235 steel during salt exposure.
At 700–900 °C, enhanced diffusion and thermal stresses make the oxide on Q235 steel porous and prone to spallation.
Porosity and spallation expose the underlying Q235 steel to aggressive salt attack.
The morphology, continuity, and adhesion of the iron-oxide scale govern corrosion degradation or protection in Q235 steel.
A defective oxide scale permits aggressive salt components to penetrate and accelerate corrosion of the underlying steel.
Molten-salt exposure at high temperature can produce measurable mass loss through corrosive attack.
Q235 steel exposed to molten salt at 700–900 °C will lose more mass than Q235 steel exposed to the salt at room temperature.
High-temperature Q235 specimens will exhibit more extensive surface degradation associated with a porous, spalled oxide.
Pre-annealing that produces a more adherent oxide will reduce the high-temperature corrosion rate of Q235 steel.
Substantial Cr, Mn, or other oxide-forming alloy additions may change corrosion behavior relative to low-alloy Q235 steel.
Steels containing substantial Cr or Mn form inherently more protective oxides.
Mass loss per unit area can be used to assess relative corrosion severity under otherwise identical salt-exposure conditions.
The protective-to-nonprotective oxide transition has an unknown temperature threshold, and the respective contributions of thermal stress and diffusion are unresolved.

contradictions.description: The room-temperature exposure is repeatedly described as a molten-salt exposure, but the conditions also call it only a 'similar salt immersion.' The physical state of the room-temperature salt is therefore inconsistent or undefined and may not match the molten exposure at 700–900 °C.

The predicted benefit of pre-annealing is conditional on formation of an improved adherent oxide, whereas the falsification rule treats any failure of pre-annealing to improve resistance as falsifying the mechanism. Failure to form the intended oxide would instead be an unsuccessful intervention and would not by itself falsify oxide-integrity control.
